clinical_category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

semantic_correction.stem: A nurse is preparing to change the dressing over a central venous catheter insertion site. Which technique best reflects current CDC recommendations?

options.A: Perform hand hygiene, use aseptic technique and recommended skin antisepsis, then apply a sterile dressing; clean or sterile gloves may be worn.
options.B: Perform hand hygiene and use clean technique; if the site looks normal, omit skin antisepsis and replace the dressing with clean nonsterile gauze.
options.C: Use sterile gloves and maximal sterile-barrier precautions for a routine dressing change, but omit skin antisepsis when the site has no drainage.
options.D: Perform hand hygiene and skin antisepsis, then apply a clean nonsterile dressing because sterility is required for insertion rather than maintenance.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC recommends hand hygiene before and after dressing an intravascular catheter and maintaining aseptic technique during catheter care. For central venous catheter dressing changes, clean skin should be prepared with a >0.5% chlorhexidine preparation with alcohol; if chlorhexidine is contraindicated, specified alternative antiseptics may be used. The catheter site should be covered with sterile gauze or a sterile transparent semipermeable dressing. CDC also states that either clean or sterile gloves may be worn when changing intravascular-catheter dressings. Maximal sterile barrier precautions are recommended for CVC/PICC insertion or guidewire exchange, not as a universal requirement for routine dressing changes. Therefore A is correct. B omits required antisepsis and a sterile dressing, C confuses insertion precautions with maintenance and omits antisepsis, and D incorrectly uses a nonsterile site dressing.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: For routine central-line dressing care, combine hand hygiene, aseptic technique, recommended skin antisepsis, and a sterile site dressing; recognize that CDC permits either clean or sterile gloves for dressing changes and reserves maximal sterile barriers for insertion-related procedures.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections — Summary of Recommendations; Background Information: Strategies for Prevention of Catheter-Related Infections
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Underlying CDC/HICPAC guideline 2011 with later recommendation updates; current CDC Summary of Recommendations page dated February 28, 2024 and Prevention Strategies page live/rechecked August 20, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Summary of Recommendations §3 Hand Hygiene and Aseptic Technique, recommendations 1, 2, and 6; §4 Maximal Sterile Barrier Precautions, recommendation 1; §5 Skin Preparation, recommendation 2; §6 Catheter Site Dressing Regimens, recommendation 1. Prevention Strategies repeats the same recommendations and clarifies their application.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: CDC recommends hand hygiene and aseptic technique for intravascular catheter dressing care, >0.5% chlorhexidine with alcohol for CVC dressing-change skin preparation unless contraindicated, a sterile catheter-site dressing, and either clean or sterile gloves for dressing changes; maximal sterile barriers apply to CVC/PICC insertion or guidewire exchange rather than routine dressing changes.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup retained the central-line dressing construct, rebuilt all four options to remove the key-length cue, and after GitHub reread removed a residual absolute-word cue from distractor C.

scope_exclusions.chlorhexidine_contraindication: The rationale preserves CDC alternatives when chlorhexidine is contraindicated; the item does not imply chlorhexidine is mandatory in every client.
scope_exclusions.pediatrics: The item does not test pediatric or neonatal chlorhexidine-impregnated dressing recommendations.
scope_exclusions.dressing_frequency: No numeric dressing-change interval is tested.
scope_exclusions.chlorhexidine_impregnated_dressing: The item tests routine aseptic dressing technique, not age- or device-specific indications for chlorhexidine-impregnated dressings.
scope_exclusions.insertion: The item is a routine dressing change, not CVC insertion or guidewire exchange.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for ‘central venous catheter dressing clean or sterile gloves aseptic chlorhexidine sterile dressing’ returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank scan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It includes all required maintenance elements without falsely requiring sterile gloves for routine dressing changes.
option_audit.B: Plausible because a normal-appearing site may seem lower risk, but CDC still requires appropriate skin antisepsis and a sterile catheter-site dressing.
option_audit.C: Plausible because maximal sterile barriers are important for CVC insertion, but they are not the routine-dressing requirement and antisepsis cannot be omitted based on site appearance.
option_audit.D: Plausible because sterile gloves are not universally required for dressing changes, but the catheter-site dressing itself should be sterile.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A is the only option that correctly combines hand hygiene, aseptic technique, skin antisepsis, sterile dressing, and the CDC-permitted clean-or-sterile glove choice.

cueing_check.note: The key is not the longest option; all four are similarly structured clinical techniques, and the residual absolute-word cue identified on first reread was removed.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: The 2026 NCSBN test plan explicitly names hand hygiene, aseptic technique, and sterile technique under Safety and Infection Prevention and Control; routine central-line dressing care directly tests these entry-level RN competencies.
blueprint_audit.visual_verification: VERIFIED. Official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan PDF pageno 11 / printed p.8 was successfully screenshot-verified August 20, 2026 and visibly contains the cited infection-prevention activity statement.
